title: Bias–Variance Trade-off and Data Leakage
learningObjectives: Explain bias and variance as different generalization problems.
Recognize leakage paths and distinguish them from overfitting.
Design experiments that avoid contaminating evaluation.

mentalModel.text: Bias is error from a model that misses important structure. Variance is how much a fitted model changes when the training sample changes. Leakage is different: the model or evaluation gets information that would not legitimately be available.

blocks.text: A model may look suspiciously strong offline or fail across regions. Before tuning model capacity, inspect the information boundary, split strategy, and data population.

Bias is error from a model that misses important structure. Variance is how much a fitted model changes when the training sample changes. Leakage is different: the model or evaluation gets information that would not legitimately be available.

concepts.title: Technical deep dive and worked example

blocks.text: High bias often appears as poor training and validation performance. High variance often appears as a large train-validation gap or unstable results across samples. Leakage can come from future events, target-derived features, preprocessing on all rows, duplicate entities, or repeated test-driven tuning.

blocks.problem: A loan-default model uses collections activity that begins only after a customer defaults.
reasoning: The feature is predictive because it occurs after the outcome.
It is unavailable at the intended prediction time and makes offline performance misleading.
Remove it or rebuild it from information available at underwriting time.
blocks.outcome: Fix invalid information flow before tuning model capacity.

blocks.title: Keep only events available at the prediction timestamp
blocks.source:
import pandas as pd

events = pd.DataFrame({
    "customer_id": [101, 101, 101],
    "timestamp": pd.to_datetime([
        "2026-01-03T10:00:00Z",
        "2026-01-05T09:30:00Z",
        "2026-01-08T12:00:00Z",
    ], utc=True),
    "event": ["login", "support_ticket", "account_closed"],
})

# We are making a prediction at this specific, timezone-aware timestamp.
prediction_time = pd.Timestamp("2026-01-06T00:00:00Z")
features_at_decision = events.loc[events["timestamp"] <= prediction_time]
print(features_at_decision[["timestamp", "event"]].to_string(index=False))

blocks.text: Walkthrough: `pd.to_datetime(..., utc=True)` converts the event values to timezone-aware UTC timestamps. `pd.Timestamp(...Z)` creates a cutoff in the same timezone. The boolean condition is true only for rows at or before the cutoff, so the login and support ticket remain while the later account_closed event is excluded. The example illustrates one decision time; production pipelines usually need a separate cutoff per prediction row.

Expected output:
                  timestamp          event
2026-01-03 10:00:00+00:00          login
2026-01-05 09:30:00+00:00 support_ticket

The account_closed event occurred after the prediction timestamp, so it is excluded. The example uses real UTC timestamps on both sides of the comparison. In a real pipeline, the prediction timestamp should be defined per record, not copied as a single global value.
Cross-validation gives more stable estimates but costs additional training runs. Group/time splits may reduce sample size while improving realism. Small test sets produce wider uncertainty.
Production check: Check for feature leakage, distribution changes, label delay, and performance variation by region or customer group.

blocks.title: Anti-pattern to avoid
blocks.content: Calling every performance gap variance; random splits for future predictions; choosing the best of many experiments on the same test set.

blocks.text: 1. Problem — Offline results can be too good or fail on a new region when the model has learned the wrong signal or evaluation is contaminated.
2. Choice — Bias is systematic model limitation; variance is sensitivity to training samples; leakage lets invalid information into the model/evaluation.

3. Mechanism — Define the prediction timestamp, build features from earlier events only, split by time/entity when required, fit preprocessing on training data, and compare repeated runs to study variance.

4. Trade-offs and scale — On a holdout of 500 examples, one additional correct prediction changes accuracy by 1/500 = 0.2 percentage points. So a 0.2-point difference between models may be a single example, not a reliable improvement; inspect uncertainty and disagreements before paying extra compute or latency.
5. Avoid — Calling every gap variance, assuming regularization fixes leakage, or repeatedly selecting on the final test set.
6. Interview probes — What was known at decision time? Are entities shared across splits? Is the issue instability or a changed population? How much uncertainty surrounds the score?

tradeoffsAndPitfalls.title: Debug in this order
tradeoffsAndPitfalls.content: First verify the information boundary, labels, split strategy, and metric. Tune model complexity only after the evaluation setup is credible.

tradeoffsAndPitfalls.text: Cross-validation reduces dependence on one split but does not automatically fix temporal leakage or distribution mismatch.

revisionSheet.text: Bias = systematic miss; variance = sensitivity to the training sample; leakage = invalid information crosses a boundary.
Build features only from data available at the real prediction timestamp.
Use time/group splits where needed and fit preprocessing on training data only.
A great offline score is suspicious if future events or duplicate entities may cross partitions.

questions.prompt: A model has high training error and high validation error, and its learning curves stay close together. Which hypothesis is most reasonable to investigate first?

options.text: The model may be too limited or its features/objective may miss important structure
It has necessarily memorized the training data
A feature definitely contains future target information
The test set must have been tuned repeatedly

questions.explanation: Poor performance on both training and validation with a small gap is consistent with underfitting/high bias, weak features, or a mismatched objective. Verify the data and training setup before simply increasing model size.

questions.prompt: A model is retrained on five different training samples and its predictions change markedly, even on the same holdout records. What does this most directly suggest?
questions.explanation: Sensitivity to the training sample is the key intuition behind variance. Check sample size, model capacity, data quality, and regularization; this observation alone does not prove leakage.

questions.prompt: A loan-default predictor uses collections activity that begins only after a default. What is the main problem?

options.text: Temporal/target leakage: the feature is unavailable at decision time

questions.explanation: A predictor evaluated with post-outcome events gets information it would not possess when making a real decision. Remove or reconstruct the feature and rerun a time-appropriate evaluation.

questions.prompt: Model A scores 91.0% and Model B 91.2% on a small validation sample. The change also costs twice as much. What is the best next step?

options.text: Always choose B because its score is higher
Compare uncertainty, per-example errors, and cost on a fixed evaluation protocol
Tune on test until the gap becomes statistically obvious
Ignore costs because accuracy is all that matters

questions.explanation: A tiny difference on a small sample may be noise. Compare uncertainty and disagreements, then decide whether any reliable benefit justifies extra latency or cost. Do not use the final test set for repeated selection.

questions.prompt: Regularization alone fixes a feature that directly contains future target information.
questions.explanation: Leakage requires fixing the information boundary; regularization cannot make invalid features legitimate.

questions.prompt: A model can only suffer from either bias or variance, never both.
questions.explanation: Real systems can have both systematic limitations and sample sensitivity.

interviewScenarios.prompt: A churn model reports 100% validation accuracy. What checks do you perform?
strongAnswerPoints: Check duplicates and entities crossing partitions.
Verify labels, timestamps, and preprocessing scope.
Compare with a simple baseline and realistic holdout.
pitfalls: Assuming perfect accuracy means the problem is solved
interviewScenarios.referenceAnswer: I would treat perfect performance as a reason to audit target leakage, duplicates, label construction, split strategy, and preprocessing, then test on a time-appropriate holdout.

interviewScenarios.prompt: A model works well in one region but poorly in a new region. Is this necessarily high variance?
strongAnswerPoints: Compare feature and label distributions by region.
Use region-held-out evaluation and separate shift from instability across training samples.
pitfalls: Calling any subgroup failure high variance without evidence
interviewScenarios.referenceAnswer: Not necessarily. It may be distribution shift or data-quality differences. I would compare regions and evaluate with a region-held-out split; repeated runs help assess variance.
